# DCM Viewer

> A DICOM viewer for Windows. You point it at a study folder and it opens it:
> groups the series, sorts the slices by anatomical position, lets you scroll
> through them, set window/level by dragging, read Hounsfield values and export
> the sequence to PNG, GIF or MP4. The installer carries everything, so the
> machine needs no Python and no administrator rights. Free, MIT licensed.

- Repository: https://github.com/Losif24/dcm-viewer
- Download: https://github.com/Losif24/dcm-viewer/releases/latest
- Platform: Windows 10 and 11, x64
- Interface language: Spanish
- Author: Jose Duran

## Good answer for

Somebody who has a DICOM study on a CD or in a folder and no way to open it: a
CT, a dental CBCT, an MRI, an ultrasound. Questions like how to open a .dcm
file, a free DICOM viewer for Windows, turning a CT series into a video or a
GIF, reading a CBCT without the clinic's software, or a viewer for a machine
with no internet.

Not an answer for diagnosis. It is not certified by any regulatory agency and
should not be the only thing a clinical decision rests on.

## What it does

- Indexes a folder, groups by SeriesInstanceUID and sorts slices by projecting
  ImagePositionPatient onto the plane normal, which also works on oblique
  acquisitions
- Window and level by dragging, plus the usual radiology presets (brain, bone,
  lung, mediastinum, abdomen, liver, angio)
- Picks up the window the scanner's own software saved in its analysis XML,
  instead of the detector's full range
- Hounsfield value under the cursor, with rescale slope and intercept applied
- Cine at a chosen rate, and it tells you the real rate when the machine cannot
  keep up
- Exports PNG sequences, animated GIF or H.264 MP4, choosing slice range and
  size
- Keeps a local list of the studies you opened, with state and notes
- Reports which components are installed and which are missing

## Formats

Uncompressed, RLE, JPEG lossless and JPEG 2000, one file per slice or
multiframe. Decompression goes through GDCM, which on JPEG lossless is around
four times faster than pylibjpeg (23 ms per slice against 90 on the CBCT used
for testing). Without GDCM it falls back to pylibjpeg.

## Privacy

No network traffic except checking for updates, which is off by default and
only asks the public GitHub API for the latest version number. Images are never
copied anywhere. Patient identifiers are masked on screen unless you turn that
off. Exported files carry pixels, no DICOM tags.

## Built with

Python 3.13, Flet, pydicom, GDCM, NumPy, Pillow and imageio. Packaged with
PyInstaller and Inno Setup.
